title: Future You
principle: Retirement and goal planning; PE/VC as the long, illiquid end
product: Emergency fund, insurance, goal SIPs, NPS, VC funds

lessons.title: Your first paycheck
lessons.subtitle: 22, and paid at last
lessons.capability: Split a first salary between needs, wants, an emergency fund and investing.

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Jump ahead with me. You're 22, and your first salary just landed: ₹30,000 a month!

steps.speaker: dash
lines: New phone, new shoes, weekend trips! Investing can wait, I'm young!

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Let's see where each choice leads. You'll split the paycheck, then live the next 18 years: a job loss, a hospital bill, a wedding, a crash.

steps.title: First Paycheck
steps.caption: Set your split, then live it. Try a few different splits.

steps.question: Which should usually come first with a new salary?

options.text: An emergency fund and health insurance
options.why: Yes. Buffers first, so one bad month doesn't become years of debt.
Debt before buffers is how small shocks become big problems.
Speculation before safety is backwards.

steps.question: Why is credit card debt so dangerous?

options.text: Interest around 36% a year compounds against you
options.why: Right. Compounding works against borrowers too.

options.text: Cards are illegal for young people
options.why: They aren't. They're just expensive if you carry a balance.
At 36% a year, a balance can double in about two years.

steps.title: In real life
steps.realLife: A common starting rule is 50/30/20: about 50% on needs, 30% on wants and 20% on saving and investing. Adjust it to your life, but pay yourself first, on payday.
steps.mission: Ask a working adult you trust: what do they wish they'd done with their first salary?
steps.deeper: Setting up SIPs to run on salary day, before you can spend, is the single most effective habit for most new earners.

lessons.title: Protect before you grow
lessons.subtitle: Insurance and the emergency fund
lessons.capability: Explain term insurance, health insurance and why they come before investing.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: Insurance is money you pay and never get back. Isn't that a waste?

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Only if nothing goes wrong. Insurance turns a disaster you can't afford into a small cost you can.
It's the hedge for your whole life plan.

items.title: Emergency fund
items.text: 3–6 months of expenses somewhere instant. Covers job loss and small shocks without selling investments.

items.title: Health insurance
items.text: Pays big hospital bills. One stay can cost lakhs without it.

items.title: Term life insurance
items.text: If you die during the term, your family gets a payout. Cheap when you're young; needed once others depend on you.

items.title: Don't mix them
items.text: Plans that bundle insurance with investing often give weak cover and weak returns. Keep them separate.

options.text: If you die during the term
options.why: Yes. That's all it does, which is why it's cheap.

options.text: A big bonus at the end
options.why: Pure term plans don't pay anything if you survive.
That's a hedge, not life insurance.

options.text: It's cheaper, and it covers you before problems appear
options.why: Right. Premiums rise with age and with existing illnesses.
Not usually. It's about cost and future cover.
It's protection, not an investment.

steps.title: Card unlocked: Insurance
steps.realLife: Insurance in India is regulated by IRDAI. Many planners suggest life cover of 10–15 times your yearly income once others rely on you, and family health cover of at least a few lakh rupees.
steps.deeper: Check the claim settlement ratio, waiting periods and exclusions before buying. A cheap policy that doesn't pay claims is worthless.

lessons.title: Retirement: the longest goal
lessons.subtitle: Start early, and the 4% rule
lessons.capability: Estimate a retirement corpus and explain why starting early matters so much.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: Retirement? I'm 16! That's a problem for old Dash.

steps.speaker: kip
lines: It's the one goal where starting early does most of the work. Compounding needs decades.
Let's see how much a ₹5,000 monthly SIP becomes, depending on when you start.

steps.title: The start-age slider
steps.caption: Slide the start age. Try raising the SIP every year.

steps.question: Waiting 10 years to start a retirement SIP…

options.text: Can cut the final pot by more than half
options.why: Yes. The last decade of compounding is the biggest.
It makes a huge difference.

options.text: Is smart, you'll earn more later
options.why: Earning more later rarely makes up for lost compounding.

options.text: How much you can take out each year in retirement
options.why: Right. Take about 4% a year and the money should last around 30 years.

options.text: How much to save each month
options.why: It's about withdrawing, not saving.
Nothing is guaranteed. It's a rule of thumb.

steps.title: Card unlocked: NPS
steps.realLife: The National Pension System, regulated by PFRDA, is a low-cost way to invest for retirement in shares and bonds. Most of it stays locked until 60, and part must buy a pension.
steps.deeper: The 4% rule came from US data. With higher inflation in India, many planners use 3–3.5% to be safe. Raising your SIP each year with your salary (a step-up SIP) makes a big difference.

lessons.title: Backing startups
lessons.subtitle: The power law of VC
lessons.capability: Explain why startup investing needs many bets, long lock-ins and only a small slice of wealth.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: Forget index funds. I'll put everything into one startup and be the next unicorn investor!

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Most startups fail. A few win huge. Venture capital funds back dozens to find those few.
Let's see what happens with one bet versus many.

steps.title: Build a VC fund
steps.caption: Slide how many startups your fund backs.

steps.question: Why do VC funds back many startups?

options.text: A few big winners pay for the many failures
options.why: Yes. That's the power law.
It's deliberate: diversification across many risky bets.
No law requires it.

steps.question: Money in a VC fund is usually…

options.why: Right. Very illiquid. Never use money you might need.
That's a savings account.
Most startups fail.

steps.title: Card unlocked: Private Equity & VC
steps.realLife: In India, most people access startups through SEBI-registered Alternative Investment Funds, which usually need at least ₹1 crore. Angel investing is also high risk. For most people it comes after everything else is in place.
steps.deeper: VC returns are extremely uneven: the top few funds earn most of the gains. Fees are high, often a 2% yearly fee plus 20% of profits.

lessons.title: Boss: Launch Day
lessons.subtitle: Everything, applied
lessons.capability: Combine buffers, protection, a sensible mix and steady investing into one plan.

steps.speaker: kip
lines: This is it. Everything you've learned, from Money Town to here, goes into one plan: your Launch Plan.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: Kip… I think I finally get it. Buffers first. Protection. Then slow and steady.

steps.title: The final paycheck
steps.caption: Make Future You thrive: no card interest, and a strong net worth at 40.

steps.brief: Launch run! Keep cash for surprises, spread across lanes and outrun The Melt one last time.

steps.question: What's the right order for a first-job plan?

options.why: Yes. Protect the downside, then grow.
Speculation first leaves you exposed.
That costs decades of compounding.

steps.question: Kip's whole philosophy in four words?

options.why: That's it. Consistency, compounding and risk you understand.
That's Dash's old motto.
Some risk is how money grows. Just the right amount, for the right time.

steps.title: World complete: Future You
steps.realLife: You've finished every world. Your Launch Plan lives in the You tab. Share it with a parent, keep your streak going, and review the ideas that slip.
steps.deeper: Real next steps at 18: a bank account in your name, KYC, and a small SIP in a broad index fund, with a parent's help.
